stories.name: Florence Nightingale
stories.title: The nurse with the lamp
lines: In 1854, Florence Nightingale went to look after soldiers in a war hospital far from home.
The hospital was dirty and crowded. Many soldiers got ill from germs, not from the fighting.
Florence and her nurses cleaned, washed, cooked good food and let in fresh air.
At night she walked round the wards with a lamp, checking on the soldiers.
She also counted. Her charts showed that most of that illness could have been stopped.
In 1860 she started a school for nurses in London, and nursing became a job you train for.

question.say: Florence's charts showed people what was really making soldiers ill. Which skill did she use?

choices.text: Using numbers to show the truth

choices.why: It wasn't luck: she counted carefully, so people believed her.
Her charts did the talking: careful numbers can change minds.

sources.fact: In 1854 she led nurses at the army hospital at Scutari; she made night rounds with a lamp, 'the Lady with the Lamp'.
Her statistics and diagrams showed most army deaths came from preventable disease; she founded the Nightingale Training School at St Thomas' Hospital in 1860.

stories.name: Mary Seacole
stories.title: Mother Seacole's hotel
lines: Mary Seacole grew up in Jamaica and learned how to care for sick people from her mother.
When a war began far away, she asked to go and help the soldiers. She was turned down.
Mary didn't give up. She paid for the long journey herself.
With a business partner she opened the British Hotel: food, warm drinks and care for tired soldiers.
When the war ended, her business was left with debts. Newspapers helped people raise money for her.
In 1857 she wrote a book about her adventures, and lots of people bought it.

question.say: Mary was told no, but she found her own way to help. Which skill did she use?

choices.text: Kept going and found another way

choices.why: She didn't stop at no: she found another way to help.
Nobody asked her: she made her own way there.

sources.fact: Turned down by the War Office, she went to the Crimea at her own expense and set up the British Hotel near Balaclava with Thomas Day; bankrupt after the war, a fund was raised for her.
Wonderful Adventures of Mrs Seacole in Many Lands was published in 1857.

stories.name: Louis Braille
stories.title: Letters you can feel
lines: Louis Braille lost his sight after an accident when he was three.
At his school for blind children in Paris, the few books had huge raised letters, slow to feel.
A soldier, Charles Barbier, had made a 'night writing' of raised dots, but it was hard to read.
So Louis made it simpler. In 1824, when he was 15, he had an alphabet of six dots.
He kept working on it for years, and became a teacher at his school.
Today, blind people all over the world read braille with their fingertips.

question.say: Louis took an idea that was hard to use and made it better. Which skill did he use?

choices.why: He didn't say impossible: he made it simpler, step by step.
He started from Barbier's idea, then kept making it better.

sources.fact: Blinded after an accident at three; at the Paris school for the blind he simplified Barbier's 12-dot night writing to a six-dot cell by 1824, aged 15; he later taught there.
Braille's system of raised dots is used worldwide by blind readers.

stories.name: Wangari Maathai
stories.title: Millions of trees
lines: Wangari Maathai grew up in Kenya and became the first woman in East and Central Africa to earn a doctorate.
She saw forests being cut down. Streams dried up, and families had less wood and food.
In 1977 she started small: the Green Belt Movement's first event planted seven trees.
She asked women to grow seedlings and plant trees, and they were paid a little for each tree that grew.
Together, they have planted more than 50 million trees.
In 2004 she became the first African woman to win the Nobel Peace Prize.

question.say: Wangari didn't plant millions of trees on her own. Which skill made it work?

choices.why: Nobody could plant millions alone. Many hands did it together.
It wasn't luck: thousands of women worked together.

sources.fact: The first female scholar from East and Central Africa to take a doctorate; founded the Green Belt Movement in 1977; the first African woman to win the Nobel Peace Prize (2004).
The movement's first event, on World Environment Day 1977, planted seven trees in Nairobi; it paid women for trees that survived.
The Green Belt Movement says it has planted over 51 million trees.

stories.name: George Washington Carver
stories.title: The teacher on wheels
lines: George Washington Carver was born into slavery. He worked hard to go to school and to college.
In 1896 he went to teach at the Tuskegee Institute in Alabama.
Farmers there grew cotton every year, and the soil got tired and poor.
He showed them how to take turns: peanuts or sweet potatoes one year, cotton the next. The soil got better.
In 1906 he started a school on wheels: the Jesup Wagon took lessons right to the farms.
He wrote simple booklets for farmers, full of ideas they could use.

question.say: Carver took his lessons out to the farms, on a wagon. Which skill did he use?

choices.why: He did the opposite: he took his lessons to everyone.
Many farmers couldn't come, so he went to them.

sources.fact: Born into slavery; head of agriculture at Tuskegee from 1896; taught crop rotation with peanuts and sweet potatoes to restore soil worn out by cotton.
The Jesup Wagon, a movable school, took Tuskegee's lessons to farmers from 1906.

stories.name: Wilbur and Orville Wright
stories.title: The brothers who learned to fly
lines: Wilbur and Orville Wright ran a bicycle shop in Dayton, Ohio. They dreamed of flying.
They built gliders and tested them on the windy sand hills of Kitty Hawk. One glider lifted much less than they hoped.
So they built their own wind tunnel, a long wooden box with a fan, and tested lots of little wing shapes.
With what they learned, they made better wings, a light engine and propellers.
On 17 December 1903, Orville flew for 12 seconds and about 37 metres: the first aeroplane flight with an engine.
Later that day, Wilbur flew for 59 seconds.

question.say: The brothers' glider didn't work as planned. Which skill did they use?

choices.why: If they had given up, there would have been no first flight.
They didn't blame anything: they tested wing shapes to find what worked.

sources.fact: Disappointed by their 1901 glider's lift, the Wrights built a wind tunnel in 1901 to test wing shapes.
17 December 1903, Kitty Hawk: the first flight was 120 feet in 12 seconds; the best that day 852 feet in 59 seconds.

stories.name: Katherine Johnson
stories.title: Check the numbers
lines: Katherine Johnson loved numbers. In 1953 she started work at Langley, the research centre that became part of NASA.
Her job was to do the sums that tell a spacecraft where to go.
In 1961 she worked out the path for Alan Shepard, the first American in space.
In 1962 John Glenn was going to fly all the way round the Earth. New electronic computers had done the sums.
Glenn asked for Katherine to check the computer's numbers. When she said they were right, he was ready to go.
In 2015 she was given the Presidential Medal of Freedom.

question.say: John Glenn trusted Katherine to check the numbers. Which skill did she use?

choices.why: A guess isn't safe for a spaceflight: she checked every step.
Asking good questions was part of her work.

sources.fact: Joined Langley in 1953; calculated the trajectory for Alan Shepard's 1961 flight; John Glenn asked her to check the electronic computer's orbit numbers in 1962; Presidential Medal of Freedom, 2015.
Glenn's request: 'If she says the numbers are good, I'm ready to go.'

stories.name: Maria Montessori
stories.title: The children's house
lines: Maria Montessori was one of the first women in Italy to become a doctor, in 1896.
She watched children very carefully, to see how they really learned.
On 6 January 1907 she opened a Children's House in a poor part of Rome, for about 60 young children.
It had child-sized tables and chairs, and things to do with your hands, so children learned by doing.
Children chose their work, tidied up and helped each other.
Her ideas spread, and there are Montessori schools all over the world today.

question.say: Maria watched children closely before she decided how to teach. Which skill did she use?

choices.why: She tried something new, from what she saw.
She didn't guess: she watched children carefully first.

sources.fact: She graduated in medicine in Rome in 1896; the first Casa dei Bambini opened on 6 January 1907 in San Lorenzo, Rome.
About 60 children aged 3 to 6 from poor families came to the first Children's House.

stories.name: Alexander Fleming
stories.title: The mould that stopped germs
lines: Alexander Fleming was a doctor and scientist at St Mary's Hospital in London.
In 1928 he came back from a holiday and looked at the dishes of germs he had left behind.
On one dish a mould had grown, and the germs round it had gone. He didn't throw it away: he looked closely.
He named what the mould made: penicillin.
Years later, a team at Oxford led by Howard Florey and Ernst Chain made it into a medicine for everyone.
In 1945 Fleming, Florey and Chain shared the Nobel Prize.

question.say: Fleming didn't throw the messy dish away. Which skill did he use?

choices.text: Noticing something odd and looking closely

choices.why: If he had tidied it away, nobody would have found penicillin then.
Surprises can be clues: he looked closely.

sources.fact: Returning from holiday in 1928, he noticed a mould that killed the bacteria around it on a culture dish, and named its substance penicillin.
The 1945 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine was shared by Fleming, Ernst Chain and Howard Florey for penicillin.

stories.name: Garrett Morgan
stories.title: The safety hood and the traffic signal
lines: Garrett Morgan's parents had been enslaved. He had only a few years of school, and taught himself to mend sewing machines.
He started his own repair shop in Cleveland, then more businesses.
He invented a safety hood to help people breathe in smoke, and got a patent for it in 1914.
In 1916, after an explosion in a tunnel under Lake Erie, he and his brother wore the hoods and went in to rescue workers.
Roads were getting busy and dangerous, so he invented a traffic signal that could stop every direction. He got its patent in 1923.
His ideas helped make rescues and roads safer.

question.say: Garrett saw dangers and made things to fix them. Which skill did he use?

choices.text: Spotting a problem and solving it

choices.why: Problems rarely go away by themselves: he invented a fix.
These were his own inventions, with his own patents.

sources.fact: Son of formerly enslaved parents, with little schooling; repaired sewing machines in Cleveland and started businesses; patented a safety hood (1914) and a traffic signal (1923).
His 1923 patent was a three-position traffic signal; in 1916 he used his hood in the Lake Erie waterworks tunnel rescue.

stories.name: Henry Dunant
stories.title: Help for everyone
lines: Henry Dunant was a Swiss businessman. In 1859, on a trip to Italy, he came to a town after a terrible battle.
Thousands of wounded soldiers lay there, with almost no one to care for them.
Henry asked the people of the town to help, and they cared for soldiers from both sides.
In 1862 he wrote a book asking every country to have helpers ready for wounded people.
In 1863 the group that became the International Committee of the Red Cross began.
Later his business went wrong and he became poor. But in 1901 he shared the very first Nobel Peace Prize.

question.say: Henry got a whole town helping, people from both sides. Which skill did he use?

choices.why: There were too many soldiers for one person: he got the town helping.
He helped everyone, from both sides.

sources.fact: A Swiss businessman who saw the wounded after the Battle of Solferino (1859) and organised help; he wrote A Memory of Solferino (1862); the International Committee of the Red Cross was founded in 1863.
He went bankrupt and lived in poverty, and shared the first Nobel Peace Prize in 1901.

stories.name: Yuan Longping
stories.title: More rice for everyone
lines: Yuan Longping grew up at a time when many people in China did not have enough food.
He wanted rice plants that gave much more rice, and he searched rice fields for unusual plants.
In 1970, he and his team found a special wild rice plant on Hainan Island, beside a railway line.
With it, they made the first high-yield hybrid rice in the 1970s: about a fifth more rice.
Hybrid rice is now grown in many countries.
He kept working in the rice fields until he was very old.

question.say: Yuan searched for years before he found the right plant. Which skill did he use?

choices.why: One try is rarely enough: he searched for years.
He didn't wait: he kept searching the fields.

sources.fact: Yuan Longping (1930-2021) developed the first hybrid rice varieties, now grown widely.
In 1970 his team found a male-sterile wild rice beside a railway line in Hainan; the hybrids of the 1970s gave about 20-30% more rice.

stories.name: Savitribai Phule
stories.title: A school for girls
lines: In India in the 1840s, most girls were not allowed to go to school.
Savitribai Phule learned to read and trained as a teacher. In 1848 she and her husband Jyotirao opened a school for girls in Pune.
Some people were angry. They threw stones and dirt at her on her way to teach.
It is said she carried a spare sari, changed at school, and taught her lessons anyway.
By 1851 they ran three schools for girls, with about 150 pupils.
She is remembered as one of India's first women teachers.

question.say: People threw dirt at Savitribai, but she kept on teaching. Which skill did she use?

choices.why: She didn't give up: the girls needed their teacher.
She didn't fight back: she kept teaching. That took courage.

sources.fact: In 1848 the Phules opened a girls' school at Bhide Wada, Pune, with Savitribai as its teacher; it is said she carried an extra sari because of what was thrown at her.
She trained as a teacher in Ahmednagar and Pune; by 1851 the Phules ran three girls' schools in Pune with about 150 pupils.

stories.name: Alberto Santos-Dumont
stories.title: Round the Eiffel Tower
lines: Alberto Santos-Dumont grew up on a coffee farm in Brazil and loved machines.
In Paris he built airships. Some broke, so he built new and better ones.
In 1901 he flew his airship number 6 round the Eiffel Tower and back, and won a big prize.
He gave the prize money away: to his workers and to poor people in Paris.
In 1906 his aeroplane, the 14-bis, flew 220 metres in Paris.
In Brazil he is remembered as a father of flying.

question.say: Alberto won a big prize and gave the money away. Which skill did he use?

choices.why: He chose to share it with the people who helped and the poor.
He gave it to his workers and to people who needed it.

sources.fact: He won the Deutsch prize in 1901 by flying round the Eiffel Tower, and gave the money to his workers and the poor of Paris; the 14-bis flew 220 metres on 12 November 1906.
On 19 October 1901 his airship No. 6 flew from Saint-Cloud round the Eiffel Tower and back for the Deutsch de la Meurthe prize.

stories.name: Fazle Hasan Abed
stories.title: Starting again, together
lines: Fazle Hasan Abed was an accountant with a good job.
In 1970 a huge storm, a cyclone, hit his country, and he went to help people on the coast.
After a war in 1971, millions of families came home to nothing.
He sold his flat in London and used the money to help families in Sulla build their homes again.
In 1972 he started BRAC. It grew to run schools, health care and small loans.
It became one of the biggest groups in the world helping people out of being poor.

question.say: Abed sold his own flat to start helping. Which skill did he use?

choices.text: Helping others with what you have

choices.why: He didn't wait: he started with what he had.
Saving is good, and he chose to use his savings to help.

sources.fact: After the 1970 cyclone he joined relief work; he sold his London flat and used the money to start work in Sulla; he founded BRAC in 1972.
A biographical sketch of Sir Fazle Hasan Abed: the cyclone, the war, the sale of his flat and BRAC.

stories.name: Fred Hollows
stories.title: Clear eyes for everyone
lines: Fred Hollows was born in New Zealand and became an eye doctor in Australia.
In the 1970s he led a team that visited more than 460 Aboriginal communities to test and treat eyes.
Many people in poorer countries could not see because of cataracts, a cloudy lens in the eye. New lenses cost a lot.
Fred worked to set up places in Eritrea and Nepal that make good lenses cheaply.
They opened soon after, and they have made millions of lenses.
The Fred Hollows Foundation, started in 1992, still helps people see.

question.say: Fred made lenses cheap, so many more people could see. Which skill did he use?

choices.text: Solving a problem for many people

choices.why: He did the opposite: cheaper lenses meant more people could see.
One at a time is kind, and he found a way to help millions.

sources.fact: Born in New Zealand; led the national trachoma and eye health programme visiting more than 460 Aboriginal communities; worked to set up lens laboratories in Eritrea and Nepal.
The Fred Hollows Foundation was launched in 1992; the lens factories opened after his death in 1993.

stories.name: Umeko Tsuda
stories.title: A girl who crossed the ocean
lines: In 1871, when she was about six, Umeko Tsuda sailed from Japan to the USA with four other girls, to go to school.
She was the youngest. She lived with a family there and studied for eleven years.
Back in Japan, she saw that few girls could go on studying after school.
She became a teacher, and went back to the USA to study more.
In 1900 she opened a school in Tokyo where young women could study English and much more.
It grew into Tsuda University.

question.say: Umeko saw that girls needed a place to study, so she started one. Which skill did she use?

choices.why: Nobody else was doing it, so she did.
She shared her learning with many young women.

sources.fact: She went to the USA in 1871 as the youngest of the girl students with the Iwakura Mission, and founded Joshi Eigaku Juku (later Tsuda College) in 1900.
She returned to Japan in 1882 and became a pioneer of women's education.

stories.name: Hassan Fathy
stories.title: Houses from mud bricks
lines: Hassan Fathy was an architect in Egypt. He wanted poor families to have good homes too.
Concrete and steel cost a lot. But mud bricks are cheap, and they keep houses cool.
He learned how builders in Nubia made curved mud-brick roofs.
He planned a new village near Luxor, New Gourna, and taught the villagers to build.
The village was never finished, and that was a big disappointment.
But he wrote a book about it, and builders in many countries still learn from his ideas.

question.say: Hassan built with cheap mud bricks instead of costly concrete. Which skill did he use?

choices.why: The poor families couldn't pay for those: he used what was there.

choices.text: Giving up when it went wrong
choices.why: When the village wasn't finished, he wrote a book so others could learn.

sources.fact: His plan for New Gourna near Luxor used mud bricks, the technique he learned in Nubia, with vaulted roofs; he taught the villagers to build; red tape prevented its completion; the book first appeared in 1969.
Architecture for the Poor: an experiment in rural Egypt (library record).

stories.name: Carlos Finlay
stories.title: Nobody believed him, at first
lines: Carlos Finlay was a doctor in Cuba. A disease called yellow fever made many people very ill there.
In 1881 he said: mosquitoes carry the disease from one person to another.
Many doctors laughed at the idea. For about 20 years, few believed him.
Carlos kept studying and explaining.
In 1900 a team led by Walter Reed tested his idea and found he was right. Reed said the discovery was Finlay's.
Getting rid of the water where mosquitoes breed helped stop yellow fever.

question.say: For about 20 years few believed Carlos, but he kept on. Which skill did he use?

choices.text: Changing his mind to fit in
choices.why: He listened, and he kept to what his evidence showed.
He kept calmly studying and explaining.

sources.fact: On 14 August 1881 Finlay proposed in Havana that mosquitoes carry yellow fever; the idea met ridicule; Walter Reed's commission confirmed it in 1900.
Reed's commission tested the mosquito idea in Cuba in 1900; mosquito control followed.

stories.name: Marie Curie
stories.title: Two Nobel Prizes
lines: Marie Sklodowska grew up in Poland, where girls could not go to university. She saved up and went to Paris to study.
With her husband Pierre, she worked for years in a cold, leaky shed, studying rays from strange rocks.
They found two new elements, polonium and radium.
In 1903 she became the first woman to win a Nobel Prize, and in 1911 she won a second one.
She is the only person to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences.
In the First World War she set up X-ray cars to help doctors look after wounded soldiers.

question.say: Marie worked for years in a cold shed to find radium. Which skill did she use?

choices.why: It took years of careful work, not luck.
She kept going when it was hard.

sources.fact: She shared the 1903 Nobel Prize in Physics, the first woman to win a Nobel Prize, and won the 1911 Prize in Chemistry for polonium and radium.
The only person to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences; in the First World War she equipped vehicles with X-ray machines for the front.
